articles.title_orig: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia
articles.content_orig:
Over the past week, Ukraine has received a stark reminder of its growing dependence on uninterrupted access to Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield networks in its drone-heavy war against Russia, now in its fifth year.
Ukraine has a fraction of Russia's resources, but its aggressive development of drone warfare on defensive and offensive fronts has helped it endure an onslaught from its much bigger adversary, which invaded Ukraine in early 2022. That was true until last week, when Ukraine reported a throttling of the Starshield network that was causing its drones to stop midflight and fall out of the sky.
The two SpaceX networks operate on a constellation of thousands of low-Earth satellites — Starlink is the commercial version, while Starshield is a military product licensed to the U.S. government and its partners, among them Ukraine.
Kyiv's reliance on drones has made Starlink and Starshield nearly indispensable to its arsenal. When Ukraine experienced a disruption to those networks, it lost the shield of interceptors and drones that offered some protection against Russian drone and missile strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes Musk throttled Starshield at the request of U.S. officials , though the world's richest man has denied any role and said it's the U.S. government that controls the military-grade network. President Trump has also denied he's responsible for slowing the network.
However, CBS News reported Tuesday that Musk was behind the disruption, which occurred after he spoke with administration officials multiple times seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, according to sources familiar with the situation.
There has also been conflicting information about whether full access to the networks has been restored. As of Wednesday afternoon, Starlink remained throttled, Zelenskyy's office confirmed.
Here's what's known about Starshield and Starlink — and their role in the Ukraine war.
On Oct. 13, Ukraine's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment, making it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones, officials and soldiers told CBS News .
Ukrainian soldiers said they noticed "speed limits" had been imposed on their use of SpaceX's Starshield internet dishes, the military-grade Starlink dishes that Ukrainians strap onto their drones so remote pilots can maintain their connection with the unmanned aircraft as they fly toward Russian targets.
Access was restricted by turning off dishes on Ukrainian drones flying above a certain speed, causing them to fall out of the sky. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense sources said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions without informing them beforehand.
Zelenskyy said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Russian Shahed attack drones.
Starshield, the military-grade satellite network, runs on the same constellation of satellites as its civilian sister, Starlink, but has fewer technical limitations and more advanced security features. Both are operated by Musk's company SpaceX.
The U.S. government pays SpaceX to license the use of Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.
There is no working alternative to Starlink, as no direct competitor approaches Starlink's coverage of 11,150 satellites. Amazon Leo aims to compete, but at this point, it has under 400 satellites in low Earth orbit and has been hampered by the launchpad explosion of a Blue Origin rocket in May.
Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr (43.5 mph) speed cap, which is the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates exceeding the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.
Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr (99.4 mph). Starshield-equipped strike drones cruise at 160 km/h or more, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.
During the throttling over the last week, Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr (55.9 mph), making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
On Oct. 15, some Ukrainian officials said that the Starshield restrictions had been lifted. But Zelenskyy told NBC News on Sunday the maximum speed was still 161 km/hr.
Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that the service was "still limited," but he added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him he would "work with his team on this to unblock" it.
It uses both. Starlink has been providing internet service to Ukrainian civilians and military forces since 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, according to Reuters .
Initially funded by private donors and a U.S. foreign aid contract, SpaceX won a Pentagon contract to pay for Starlink for Ukraine in 2023, along with a contract for 500 Starshield terminals.
In August 2024, SpaceX signed another Defense Department contract to expand Starshield usage to 3,000 terminals for the front lines, Bloomberg reported.
Beyond communicating with and guiding drones over long distances, Starshield also serves another function: It connects every sensor and weapon system on the battlefield. Disruptions to the service have an impact that can be compared to an office having to function without being able to connect to Wi-Fi.
Ukraine's military uses Starlink for general battlefield communications, and Ukrainian civilians rely on it for communications needs, too.
On the Russian side, the Kremlin had also been using Starlink until February, when SpaceX cut off its access. As a result, Ukraine gained more than 150 square miles of territory.
CBS News reported Tuesday that a decision by Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, though it remains unclear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.
Musk had spoken with administration officials multiple times, seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, sources said. He has in the past expressed distaste for the perception that his company could be seen as profiting from the Ukraine war.
The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some Trump administration officials, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon had specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.
The president said Monday he was seeking information about who had ordered the slowdown. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday denied the Pentagon had manipulated the service, saying, "We haven't made any directives or anything like that."
Musk has not admitted to imposing restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the world's richest person wrote on X .
He added that Starlink is a "commercial service," writing that it is "limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action."
Rubio, however, seemed to attribute the network constraints to Musk.
"The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk," Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Wednesday.
Within a few minutes, though, he seemed to concede that Starshield was different: "We don't control what a private company — how they decide their product can be used.  Now, if they're in a contract with the United States military, like Starshield, that's a different matter, because that's something we are purchasing and using for our use."
At around the same time as the Starlink and Starshield disruptions, Ukraine also did not receive warnings from U.S. intelligence about major Russian strikes.

articles.title_orig: Airbnb guests freed from chores involving ‘significant effort’ under new global rules
articles.title_zh: Airbnb guests freed from chores involving ‘significant effort’ under new global rules
articles.content_orig:
Accommodation platform acts after long-standing guest complaints over doing dishes, taking out rubbish and stripping beds
Airbnb hosts will no longer be able to ask guests to strip beds or wash dishes under the accommodation platform’s new rules.
The changes, which apply to Airbnb reservations covered by the platform’s global policy, will come into effect on 20 November and limit chores imposed on guests.
Airbnb had long fielded complaints from guests about having to pay cleaning fees, which can be hundreds of dollars, and still complete a list of chores for their host.
Since April 2025, cleaning fees have not been shown to guests. Instead, hosts have been allowed to choose to factor cleaning costs into the total price of the stay.
In a community policy update posted on its website this week, Airbnb said hosts would “generally” no longer be allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that “require significant effort or time or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.
Examples of such tasks include stripping beds of linen, taking rubbish offsite, and washing and putting away dishes, the company said.
The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules which must be displayed in full at the time of booking – and can also add other “reasonable” requests.
Examples of house rules include check in and check out times, limits on how many guests can stay at the property, smoking restrictions, quiet hours, and whether or not pets are allowed.
Reasonable requests depend on “relevant local considerations”. For example, it may be reasonable to ask guests to limit shower time due to local water restrictions, or to dispose of rubbish in an animal-proof container.
after newsletter promotion
While guests shouldn’t be asked to wash and put away dishes under the new guidelines, hosts can ask them to put used dishes in the sink.
“House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we’ve heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage,” an Airbnb spokesperson said.
“So we’ve redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises.”

articles.title_zh: Nasdaq tumbles on AI spending concerns and jump in oil prices: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks tumbled slid on Thursday on renewed concerns around spending by artificial intelligence companies, while while oil prices jumped as geopolitical tensions rise.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite pulled back 2.1%, while the S&P 500 shed 1.3%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 279 points, or 0.5%.
Meta Platforms slipped 5% even it exceeded revenue expectations and offered upbeat guidance. Technology more broadly was under pressure as well as ongoing concerns about artificial intelligence spending persisted. Advanced Micro Devices fell more than 5%, while Micron Technology and Nvidia dropped 2% and 1%, respectively.
Neocloud leader CoreWeave , whose bond yields and credit default swaps remain elevated , declined nearly 4% as well. The move comes as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that demand for neoclouds is " off the charts ." However, he added that capital is scarce and impeding growth.
Huang's commentary about a scarcity of capital is "spooking markets and reigniting the concerns around the capital markets on the credit side being full from a risk appetite standpoint," said Wells Fargo traders in a note. They also said Meta's comments about the large amount of AI funding needed caused the shares to roll over and weighed on overall market.
JPMorgan traders noted that Wednesday's bullish "tone reversed overnight" because Meta shares rolled over in the premarket and chatter increased "over renewed Iran kinetic-risk post US mid-term election."
Additionally, "underlying price actions and feedback from our trading desk also suggested the still fragile narrative around AI financing concerns and the lack of conviction/re-grossing from the recent tech reversal," they said in a note to clients.
Oil prices, meanwhile, jumped after The New York Times reported, citing sources, that the U.S. and Israel have plans for renewed strikes against Iran following next month's midterm U.S. elections. President Donald Trump also told reporters late Wednesday that Washington is not negotiating with Tehran and that something will happen "fairly soon."
International benchmark Brent crude futures traded 3% higher at above $112.45 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate crude futures advanced 2% to above $99.95 per barrel.
Investors also turned to U.S. Treasurys in their search for a safe haven. The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield dropped more than 9 basis points to 5.048%. The 2-year note yield also shed 9 basis points to trade at 4.733%.
Shares of CME Group advanced 3% on the back of an upgrade by JPMorgan.
The bank re-rated the stock to overweight from underweight and increased its December 2027 price target on the stock to $367, up from their prior $250.
JPMorgan analyst Kenneth Worthington describer the current interest rate environment as "constructive" for further growth in CME's interest rate business since the company benefits when CME activity when longer term rates are rising.
He also favors CME's launch of a series of new products, which could "evolve into larger opportunities," citing its successful launch of its crypto futures service.
The analyst also cites CME's expansion in some cases to 24/7 trading for pre-existing retail-sized contracts.
Rollins reported weaker-than-expected third-quarter results as the pest control company continued to face challenges attracting residential customers.
Revenue rose 6.2% from a year earlier to $1.09 billion, while adjusted earnings came in at 33 cents per share. Analysts polled by FactSet expected a profit of 34 cents per share on revenue of $1.11 billion.
"We are disappointed with our third quarter performance and are acting with urgency to address the challenges impacting our results. We now have a clearer understanding of how the customer acquisition landscape is evolving and are taking concrete steps to optimize our approach," said President and CEO Jerry Gahlhoff Jr.
To be sure, the stock rose more than 4%.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 218 points, or 0.4%. The S&P 500 shed 0.9%, and the Nasdaq Composite pulled back 1.5%.
Shares of Lockheed Martin rose more than 3% after the company reported better-than-expected results for the third quarter. Driven by strong demand for fighter jets and missile defense systems, Lockheed also hiked its earnings and revenue guidance for 2026.
The company now expects 2026 ⁠sales of about $80 billion to $82 billion, up from its previous outlook of $79.75 billion to $81.75 billion.
Sales for the defense contractor touched $20.6 billion, an increase of 11% from a year earlier. Lockheed's order backlog jumped to a record $292 billion, boosted by a $52.5 billion multiyear contract for PAC-3 missile interceptors amid heightened global defense demand.
Shares of Procter & Gamble added around 3% in premarket trading after the consumer goods company posted a beat on both the top and bottom lines for its fiscal first quarter..
The Tide and Pampers parent saw adjusted earnings of $2 per share, topping the $1.88 consensus estimate, according to LSEG. Revenue came in at $23.28 billion, above the $22.80 billion expected from analysts.
Procter & Gamble also raised its full-year revenue guidance to a range of 2% and 4%, up from its prior guidance of 1% to 3%.
"While we expect there will continue to be geopolitical and economic challenges, this strong start keeps us on track to deliver within our guidance ranges for organic sales growth, core EPS growth and free cash flow productivity for the fiscal year," CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said in a statement.
Initial filings for unemployment insurance slipped last week to their lowest level since mid-July, the Labor Department reported Thursday.
Jobless claims totaled a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ending July 18, down 6,000 from the prior period and below the Dow Jones consensus for 200,000. That was the lowest total since July 18 as employers remain reluctant to let go of employees even as hiring as slowed.
Continuing claims, which run a week behind, rose 25,000 to 1.73 million.
President Donald Trump told reporters Wednesday night  the U.S. is not negotiating with Iran but added "something will happen fairly soon." His comments come as investors worry about escalating tensions in the region following the midterm elections in November.
Asked whether the neocloud business model is on shaky ground, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC on Thursday that capital for the sector is scarce.
"There's a scarcity of capital. The demand [for] the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital," Huang said.
An analysis from Gartner put out last week found that as much as $3.5 trillion in investment spending could be on the rocks due to insufficient profitability for AI software. Large scale consolidation among AI-dedicated providers of computing power could ensue.
By 2030, more than 80% of neoclouds could cease functioning as independent businesses and be susceptible to some form of takeover, Gartner warned.

In a video statement published on his X account, Saree claimed the attacks were carried out using ballistic missiles and drones, with direct hits on all four targets.
"The criminal Saudi enemy has carried out, during its aggression and latest escalation over the past 100 days, more than 2,900 airstrikes and missile attacks targeting civilian objects in our beloved country," he said. The Houthis "will continue their operations deep inside Saudi Arabia in defence of our country and our people," he added.
Anti-American propaganda is a common sight on the streets of the Iranian capital, but authorities have gone a step further with their latest effort – a life-size jail cell with an actor playing President Trump languishing inside.
The 3D art installation is proving a hit with locals, who have been stopping to take selfies as well as hurl abuse at the pseudo-Trump.
Since the ongoing war began with joint American and Israeli strikes on Feb. 28, Iran has ramped up its propaganda operations. In the new campaign, a mock-prison cell is suspended several stories high over Tajrish Square, in an upscale neighborhood of north Tehran.
The actor, wearing a prosthetic mask to look like Mr. Trump, paces around the cell or clutches its bars. A screen set up nearby shows messages denouncing alleged U.S. war crimes .
Tehran's municipal authorities, which are behind the campaign, have said the objective is to remind the capital's residents of Iran's demands for justice .
The Saudi-led coalition fighting on behalf of Yemen's government in the neighboring country's spiraling civil war said Thursday that four more drones were intercepted over the capital and the hold city of Medina.
The force did not attribute the attacks to anyone, but the drones were likely launched by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels, who have peppered Saudi Arabia with deadly strikes in recent weeks, with many projectiles getting through the kingdom's defenses .
Earlier Thursday the Saudi coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed one drone over Riyadh, again without saying where it had come from.
The Houthis have repeatedly denied targeting Medina or Mecca, the two holiest cities in Islam.
The shadow fleet of tankers holding Iran's offshore oil reserves, which it had been selling to China throughout the war against the U.S. and Israel, have run dry, intelligence firm Kpler told The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday.
The millions of barrels of crude, held on dozens of oil tankers in Asian water, ran out in mid-October, Kpler told the outlet, with a U.S. naval blockade preventing Iran from replacing the crude being sold to Chinese refineries.
"There's no more oil to discharge to China anymore," said Homayoun Falakshahi, head of crude-oil analysis at the firm.
The U.S. naval blockade has cost Iran at least $25 billion in oil revenue, according to U.S. Central Command.
Egypt's Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty on Thursday said all options must be explored to find a political solution between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
At a press conference where he reiterated solidarity with Saudi Arabia, he stressed "the necessity of exploring all avenues for reaching political solutions."
The conflict between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and the Iran-backed Houthis erupted in summer and has drastically escalated in recent weeks.
Egypt announced Sunday that it was prepared to provide military assistance to Saudi Arabia .

In a statement published on X , Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the group's forces were carrying out rescue operations and would provide further information later.
"The Saudi enemy targets an Indian yacht near Zuqar Island, with 14 people of Indian nationality on board, according to preliminary information," he wrote in his post.
"This reckless act by the Saudi enemy in targeting the yacht threatens international navigation in the Red Sea, and the international community must stop the Saudi enemy from these reckless actions," said Saree.
There was no further information or other reports available to corroborate the Houthis' claim.
The Commander-in-Chief of the Iranian Army, Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami, said Thursday that the country's armed forces were prepared for asymmetric warfare and satisfied with their drone capacity.
"In the previous asymmetric war, we fought the enemy with equipment that surprised them, as they received very heavy blows," he said, referring to the intense exchange of fire with the U.S. and Israel before a June ceasefire was announced. That deal, which President Trump soon declared over , failed to bring about the negotiations on Iran's nuclear program and many other issues that it provisioned, but neither side has engaged in major strikes since the summer, with fighting in the region largely shifting to the linked conflict in Yemen.
"We have reached a good level of maturity in the field of drones and unmanned systems," Hatami said. "We assure our dear people of Iran that we are in a good position."
Top European diplomats will hold talks in Istanbul Friday with their counterparts from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt during a meeting initiated by Ankara, a Turkish foreign ministry source told the AFP news agency on Thursday.
Foreign ministers from the so-called E3 group – Britain, France and Germany – will meet counterparts from the newly created R4 group to discuss the Palestinian issue, developments in Yemen and the Strait of Hormuz and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine war, the source said.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will host the meeting, the first to bring together the two groups.
"The seven countries will come together for the first time in the R4+E3 format, at Turkey's initiative," the source said, indicating they would explore "opportunities for cooperation and coordination that could be put into practice ... in the coming period."
In chairing the meeting, Fidan was expected to focus on the international community "increasing pressure on Israel" in response to its settlement expansion and its "encouragement of settler terrorism," the source AFP.
Fidan will also underline support for Saudi Arabia's security in the face of attacks by Yemen's Houthis, and stress the need for permanent freedom of navigation in the Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Straits.

articles.title_zh: Tesla shares slip after capex cut raises doubts over Musk's AI and robotics push
articles.content_orig:
Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday, even as automotive revenue dropped. The stock slid more than 3% in extended trading.
Here's how the company did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:
Tesla's earnings report lands a day after CEO Elon Musk told investors on SpaceX's quarterly call that it would be a "good idea" for his two companies to merge, and said the boards at both have formed special committees to discuss a possible tie-up.
"I feel like I'm tap dancing through a minefield," Musk said on the call, responding to a question about a potential merger.
Musk addressed the matter in his opening comments on the Tesla call, but didn't provide any additional information.
"I think I said everything that should be said yesterday," he said.
Tesla's revenue was down slightly flat from a year earlier, when the company generated sales of $28.24 billion, according to the earnings deck. In Tesla's core automotive business, revenue declined 3% from a year earlier to $20.56 billion in the quarter. Energy revenue fell 16% to $2.88 billion.
Balancing out the declines were gains in Tesla's services and other revenue. Sales there climbed 33% from a year ago to $4.61 billion.
Tesla blamed its lackluster automotive revenue and profits on lower average sales prices for its cars during the quarter, and trouble securing battery supplies to make enough vehicles to fulfill a backlog of orders.
Net income attributable to common share holders plummeted 29% to $787 million, or 22 cents a share, from $1.11 billion, or 32 cents a share, a year earlier, Tesla said.
The drop in profitability reflects a surge in spending on Optimus humanoid robots and other artificial intelligence initiatives. Capital expenditures more than doubled from a year earlier to $3.73 billion. Free cash flow plunged by 62% year over year to $1.53 billion, after Tesla turned free cash flow negative in the second quarter.
Tesla said uptake of its FSD (Supervised), a partially automated driving system the company sells for $99 per month in the U.S., grew by 20 percentage points from the second quarter. Active FSD subscriptions increased 67% from a year earlier to 1.74 million.
"We believe that FSD is driving demand in markets where it is available, and we continue to work with regulators to get it approved in other markets," the company said in its investor deck.
Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's vice president of Autopilot, said on the earnings call that the company plans to give some customer cars access to its forthcoming FSD (Unsupervised) systems around the second quarter of next year.
Tesla is testing its Cybercab, a bronze two-seater designed for use as a robotaxi, but it's not yet sold to individuals. Musk said on the call that "the vast majority of the Cybercab stuff will be essentially Tesla-owned and transport-as-a-service."
The company plans to bring Cybercab to cities beyond Austin, Texas, this year, Taneja said, paying attention to operating costs like maintenance, charging and cleaning.
Musk said the company's driverless Robotaxi fleet will start to contribute to the company's financials in 2027. That fleet now includes 362 Model Y Robotaxi, and 449 Cybercab vehicles authorized for driverless operations in Texas, according to the state's Department of Motor Vehicles,
"It's not like going to move the needle this quarter," Musk said, "I think it starts to become noticeable in Q2 and then probably a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year."
Barring regulatory intervention and protectionism, Musk predicted that Tesla "will end up doing a majority of all passenger miles on Earth in any country where it is allowed to operate freely."
Tesla said its auto sales in Canada, Japan, Taiwan and Australia hit new records during the quarter. However, the company has gotten meager growth out of its core market of late as Chinese EV makers such as BYD and Xiaomi gained popularity in Asia and Europe with affordable and innovative EVs. Tesla was also hit last year by the end of a federal EV tax credit.
Earlier this month, Tesla reported vehicle deliveries for the third quarter of 486,532, about 2% below the year-ago number. Deliveries are the closest approximation of sales reported by Tesla but are not precisely defined in its shareholder communications.
One of Tesla's big investments is in a semiconductor factory that it's building with SpaceX and Intel in Grimes County, Texas. That partnership with SpaceX along with other areas of overlap, including work on Tesla's recently announced Roadster refresh, fueled intensifying speculation that Musk's companies were on the verge of combining in what would be a historic transaction.

articles.content_orig:
Only authorised union protests will be allowed in French towns and cities on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron has said, after demonstrations across the country turned violent last weekend.
Speaking as some cities including Lyon and Nice imposed complete bans, Macron said "illegitimate" protests would not be allowed but unions would be offered alternative routes so that businesses could be protected.
Big demonstrations against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed last Saturday by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed.
Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared to last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest.
France's justice minister said on Thursday that 217 people had been jailed over last weekend's disorder after being convicted in fast-track trials, with that number expected to rise.
Gérald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been arrested across France and more than 1,000 have appeared in court.
Half of those detained had no prior criminal record, he said, according to Le Figaro newspaper.
Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday.
"The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced. "When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned."
He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic".
Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm.
The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned.
In Lyon, France's third-biggest city, regional authorities have imposed a blanket ban on demonstrations.
"In light of the mobilisation that is circulating and in view of the events of 17 October, the prefect has decided to prohibit by decree any demonstration in the city of Lyon this Saturday," the Rhône prefecture said in a statement.
Similar announcements have been made in Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east.
Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds.
Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests .
Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction.
Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests.
Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the office, housed in a 19th-Century building, was "a tragedy".
In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started.
The iconic Place de la République was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc.
Following the unrest, France's interior minister Laurent Nuñez tendered his resignation, which was rejected by President Macron.
The Élysée Palace asked him instead to look at how to make France's streets safer and bring rioters to justice.
Nuñez said his teams had forecast 200,000 demonstrators, a figure much lower than the 550,000 estimated to have gathered.
The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year.

As a longtime user of the original, Neil was excited to see what the new COROS DURA 2 SOLAR had in store. His review dives into his impressions of the new head unit, how it differs from the much-beloved debut model, and whether the price jump is worth it for those considering the upgrade. Find his full video and written reviews below…
Additional photos by Logan Watts
Today, we’re looking at a new head unit, the COROS DURA 2 SOLAR. It looks unlike any I’ve ever seen. In my latest review, I’ll be diving into the details you need to know, including the specs, some interesting new features, a few major head-scratchers, and my first impressions. Check out my full video review followed by a written version below.
The original DURA was, and still is, an amazing head unit. It has the best battery life of any head unit I’ve ever used, a simple interface in a sea of increasingly complicated options, and, best of all, a very affordable $250 price tag. COROS made a splash in the cycling world, and the DURA became one of the best head units for bikepacking. In fact, I’ll say it: for trips longer than three days, it’s my first choice because of its battery life. Before the first DURA release, COROS wasn’t exactly a household name in cycling. Despite its success, it still might not be a household name. But it gained plenty of recognition for delivering a head unit that lasts a ridiculously long time without breaking the bank, giving it a solid foothold in a saturated industry.
That said, COROS released the first DURA before it was truly ready. Maybe that’s why the price tag was so enticing. Did it get the job done? Yes. But as I mentioned in my *original review*, there were some hiccups. I held off on reviewing it until a few firmware updates had addressed enough of those issues. Doing a first look at the DURA 2 SOLAR hurts a little, because I know I haven’t put it through the kind of testing I normally would for a full review. But most of those early growing pains seem to be behind us. And during my initial testing, the DURA 2 has felt much more refined and ready for market. And yes, it’s pretty darn weird-looking.
The unit comes in a nice box. Open it up, and you’ll find the DURA 2 SOLAR with stickers identifying the dials and buttons. It also comes with a lanyard to wrap around the bars or stem for security, which I always use with head units. I appreciate that COROS still includes what looks like a quality, long USB-C to USB-C cable and a bunch of instructions. Oddly enough, my test unit didn’t come with a mount. Logan got the new aluminum one, and he said it’s well-made and sleek, and it comes with a GoPro-style undermount option for lights or a camera.
Since plenty of customers already have mounts, you can buy the unit on its own or pay extra for a version with a mount. I asked COROS to send me one, but it didn’t arrive in time. Packaging isn’t a major factor in the overall experience of any piece of tech, but it’s well done here: clean, nearly all recyclable, and thoughtfully put together. Many cycling head unit companies have dialed that in over the last few years, and I appreciate it.
The DURA 2 SOLAR is a big departure from the original unit. The original unit positioned itself as a budget option amid increasingly expensive computers. I don’t know if this was the plan all along, but bringing an affordable head unit into a market with so few budget options made a lot of sense. Add the incredible battery life, and the original DURA was a unicorn. But breaking into the cycling industry as a relatively unknown brand isn’t easy. COROS mentioned that DURA sales were a little slow at first, but picked up as more people learned about the price and user feedback and reviews started rolling in.
Instead of updating the DURA and maintaining that price point, COROS decided to go premium. I’ll admit it’s a little disappointing, especially since they’re discontinuing the original. I’m sad to see that option go, and it feels like a massive miss. Let’s hope they bring a lower-budget option to the table, but I’m not holding my breath. If anything, I think they might drop “SOLAR” from the product name and launch a non-solar unit at a slightly lower price, but that would eliminate one of the new unit’s best features.
I’ve always thought of COROS as a brand for the people. I’ve used their watches for three years now, and between the features, battery life, and price, they’re pretty hard to beat. It gave me the impression that a brand could build good products, deliver a strong user experience, and still make a profit without charging top dollar. That said, the DURA 2 SOLAR comes in at $499 without a mount or $549 with one. That puts the unit alone at roughly twice the price of the first DURA, which launched just two years ago. Inflation aside, that’s a pretty big jump. So, let’s dive into the differences and see whether the new one is worth it.
The new DURA 2 SOLAR is a looker. It uses a carbon-and-alloy construction, compared to the first DURA’s mostly plastic body, and they weigh about the same: 100 grams for the DURA 2 SOLAR and 101 grams for the other. The overall shape is strange. It almost looks like a concept car, and COROS seems to be leaning into aerodynamics. The upper portion is only 5.7mm thick, easily the thinnest of any head unit I’ve tested. It thickens toward the main body near the quarter-turn mount. It’s similar in width to the original but significantly longer, measuring 117mm long, 58mm wide, and 17mm thick. Overall, it feels nice in the hand and is fairly lightweight. Once you attach it to the quarter-turn mount, it sits nicely out front. From the top, it doesn’t look nearly as ridiculous as it does from the side.
The controls have changed too. It has two physical buttons, one on each side, but the oversized watch-style scroll dial is gone, which I really enjoyed using. Now you get two haptic buttons at the bottom, plus an updated touchscreen that feels much more sensitive and responsive than the original. You can also charge the device using the USB-C port below the right button. The larger 3.5” display is a welcome change. This was one of my complaints with the original, especially when navigating: it seemed like they could have fit a larger screen into the body. I think they’ve done a good job addressing that here. In my initial testing, the touchscreen works well, and I like the haptic feedback. And paired with the side buttons, it’s intuitive and relatively simple to use.
Speaking of the screen, the DURA 2 SOLAR still uses a sunlight-readable, Memory-in-Pixel, or MIP, display designed for low power consumption. Howeve

Replacing an employee means addressing the many different tasks within their job, deploying AI that can perform those tasks reliably at scale, and adapting those systems as workflows evolve. If that doesn’t happen, companies can find themselves with fewer people but without technology genuinely doing the work they removed.

(Kitco News) - The gold market is struggling below $4,100 an ounce and could face further selling pressure as the U.S. labor market remains relatively healthy, with fewer American workers applying for unemployment benefits than expected.
Initial claims for state unemployment benefits came in at a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ending October 17, the Labor Department announced Thursday. The number was below expectations, as consensus estimates forecast a steady 200,000 claims. The previous week’s figure was revised up to 200,000.
Jobless claims have fallen to their lowest level since late July.
Spot gold has been on the back foot through most of the European session, and while prices have recovered from their session lows, the market continues to face significant selling pressure. Gold last traded at $4,076 an ounce, down 1.5% on the day.
The four-week moving average for new claims – often viewed as a more reliable measure of the labor market since it flattens week-to-week volatility – dropped to 197,750, following the previous week’s revised 198,500 level.
Analysts have noted that gold remains in a challenging position as persistent inflation has forced the Federal Reserve to adopt a new tightening bias. The latest labor market data gives the central bank room to deal with rising consumer prices.
“Layoffs aren’t picking up, and after PPI at 6.3% that gives the Fed no reason to ease,” said  Waleed Said, Technical Analyst at GivTrade.
However, Waleed added that the U.S. labor market also has its limits in the current economic environment.
“The detail most will miss: continuing claims rose to 1.728M, so people who lose their jobs are taking longer to find new ones. Firing is low, but hiring is slowing,” he said.
Said explained that the current environment will remain negative for gold.
“A strong labor print plus a hawkish Fed is pressuring gold even with a war going on, and that tells you rates are driving the market right now,” he said.
Monte Safieddine, Head of Market Research at Capital.com, said that with gold prices below $4,100 an ounce, the market now needs to hold critical support at $4,000 an ounce.
“It is a confidence test. Speculators are trying to defend it because a clean break below would signal that the market has stopped pricing rate relief and started pricing sticky inflation, elevated yields, and a stronger dollar,” he said. “The real risk for gold is that geopolitics is becoming inflationary rather than simply defensive. Any further escalation on the geopolitical front risks pushing oil even higher. Gold is trapped between two opposing forces: fear should support it, but oil-led inflation is giving central banks less room to cut. Unless the geopolitical shock is severe enough to trigger a full risk-off event, the first market reaction may be higher crude and higher yields, not a sustained gold rally.”

articles.title_orig: A Typography Geek Pointed Out Something About The Space Shuttle Discovery And Now I Can't Unsee It
articles.title_zh: A Typography Geek Pointed Out Something About The Space Shuttle Discovery And Now I Can't Unsee It
articles.content_orig:
Even though I was born in the Apollo Era, barely, the spacecraft that I think had the most influence on my childhood had to be the Space Shuttles. I remember poring over diagrams and drawings of the shuttles in National Geographic foldouts, where they even took my attention from the Forbidden Nipples seen on some of the other pages. I remember watching that first launch of the shuttle Colombia in 1981, I remember the tragedy of the Challenger in 1986, and I remember covering the process of moving the orbiter Endeavour through the streets of Los Angeles to its eventual home at the California Science Center. And more recently, I’ve taken my kid to see the orbiter Discovery at the Udvar-Hazy Center just outside of Washington, DC.
It’s that orbiter that I want to talk about specifically, because I saw a social media post about the orbiter Discovery that grabbed my attention and held it with the sort of fierce grip I imagine Miss Piggy employs on Kermit’s impossibly thin limbs when they’re alone.
That post was on Threads, and I just figured out how to embed a post from that site, so here, you can see it for yourself:
Wait, what? Discovery has an upside-down ‘s’ in its name? How the hell did that happen? Discovery was usually considered, by astronauts and NASA people, the jewel in the Space Shuttle crown. It was recognized to be the most reliable and best-performing of all the orbiters, and had the most missions and time in space . Since it was first launched in 1984, Discovery completed 39 missions, spent in total a full year in space, and traveled 150 million miles.
The thing flew for 27 years, and somehow nobody noticed that the ‘s’ was upside down on the starboard side name text?
I mean, I guess I should be more understanding; I’ve seen it several times and never noticed, and it wasn’t until just tonight that I looked back at some old photos I took of Discovery the last time I was there and saw, holy crap, the dude on Threads was right. That ‘s’ is rotated 180°.
Now, the typography on the shuttle orbiters follows NASA’s carefully-planned and strictly-enforced graphic and typographic guidelines , which state that the typography used on the spacecraft should be Helvetica Medium:
Okay, let’s take a look at the typography on the orbiter:
(the ‘r’ on the font I used there feels a bit different, too, but this gets the point across and I have to get on a flight in a few hours so I’m gonna let that slide)
It’s a subtle difference, but as you can see, the starboard side’s name definitely has that flipped ‘s.’ It’s subtle, but the Helvetica ‘s’ is slightly wider on the bottom, giving the letter a somewhat more settled appearance. Here, look:
You can see the difference there, right? I feel like once it’s pointed out, you can’t help but notice it. The ‘v’ on the port side looks oddly thick, too, now that I’m looking at it.
I’ve been told that the graphics on these orbiters was applied using large stencils and special space-grade paint, and I’m sure the complex curves of the fuselage didn’t make the application of these elements easy. It’s understandable that a letter stencil may have been flipped around, but I am sort of surprised it was never corrected in its 27 years of service life.
All the other graphics and typography are applied with impressive precision; maybe there were people who knew that ‘s’ was wrong, but kind of liked that subtle imperfection, as it does add character to the spacecraft. I get that, absolutely. If I was in charge, I’d have just let it ride, too.
I still can’t believe I’d never clocked this before; as a typographic geek and a space geek who has spent far too much time looking at pictures of spacecraft in books and online, you’d think I’d have encountered this before, but, nope. Or if I did, it didn’t make enough of an impression to consciously note it or remember.
But now that it’s there? I can’t unsee it. And I’m sort of delighted by that.
I am not sold. The word lies. on two planes, joined by an angled convex rib. The pics where it looks upside down are all from below the belt line, and the upper part is skewed more and differently from the lower.
I’d like to see pics from above the belt line. And considering other comments, from above the belt line on similar dates.
In a zero gravity environment, the S can work in many directions.
Letters were applied by a Jeep owner and typography enthusiast. Somewhere on the shuttle is a bumper sticker readingIif the starboard s reads I upside down, flip me over.”
Maybe it was like what the carpenters did with staircase spindles. An old religious tradition holds that only God can create true perfection. Carpenters would intentionally leave one spindle upside down to show humility and acknowledge that human work always has flaws.
When Discovery was delivered to the Smithsonian, they first did a flyover of the National Mall. I was lucky enough to be working at a building on the Mall at the time, with legitimate access to the roof. Best day on the job.

articles.title_orig: Who blinked first? Fragile EU-China trade peace sparks new war of words
articles.title_zh: Who blinked first? Fragile EU-China trade peace sparks new war of words
articles.content_orig:
As European officials flag more trade restrictions, Beijing bristles at the idea it can be pushed into yielding to Brussels’ demands
In Brussels and Berlin, officials are emboldened by what they consider proof that collective EU pressure can force Chinese concessions. Rather than resting on their laurels, they are cooking up a fresh batch of trade restrictions.
Beijing, on the other hand, has bristled at the idea that it can be strong-armed into yielding to Europe’s demands, even more so the suggestion that further concessions may be coming. State media has carried numerous warnings against European hubris.
It has resulted in an awkward, terse trade peace: an agreement that was supposed to defuse a trade war has led to both sides, rhetorically at least, hardening their positions. With verbal volleys flying back and forth, doubts are already surfacing over whether this delicate ceasefire can hold until the next round of negotiations in January.

articles.title_orig: American Express brings Airbnb bookings and rewards to Amex Travel platform
articles.title_zh: American Express brings Airbnb bookings and rewards to Amex Travel platform
articles.content_orig:
American Express is bringing Airbnb into its travel rewards platform.
The companies on Thursday announced a new partnership to bring more than 1 million Airbnb listings to Amex's travel portal and allow cardholders to earn rewards when booking the stays. It does not currently allow members to redeem points to pay for Airbnb bookings.
The launch adds Airbnb rentals to Amex's hotel portfolio, which includes more than 3,400 properties across its Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection programs.
Amex members with either the consumer or business Platinum card can also now apply their $600 annual lodging credit — previously called the hotel credit — to Airbnb's higher-end Luxe stays and take advantage of a new $250 statement credit on eligible Airbnb Experiences after making a Luxe booking.
"We're excited to bring more choice and flexibility to American Express Card Members with this exclusive partnership. Both of our companies exist to help people travel more and better, and this partnership helps people see more of the world by making travel more rewarding," said Juan David Borrero, head of partnerships at Airbnb, in a news release.
Membership points vary by card:
The changes come as competition among premium credit cards continues to ramp up.
Last year, American Express raised the annual fee on its premium Platinum card to $895. In turn, it's been investing in cardholder perks such as new lounges in airports and at big-ticket events and experiences as a way to attract more high-paying customers.
Earlier this month, it announced an expansion of its Centurion Lounges , with renovations coming to four existing lounges and new ones planned for Newark Liberty International Airport and London Heathrow Airport. The Newark lounge will be the largest in its network.
The partnership also comes as Americans continue to opt for travel and luxury experiences, even as prices for airfare, gas and hotels rise. Despite higher costs, more than half of Americans reported making no changes to their travel plans this summer , a recent study by travel insurance company Squaremouth found.

articles.title_orig: Horrifying video shows Mexican teen falling to her death from carnival ride
articles.title_zh: Horrifying video shows Mexican teen falling to her death from carnival ride
articles.content_orig:
A Mexican teenager died after falling from a carnival ride, with horrific video showing her flying out of her seat as the ride reached full speed.
Gabriela Rodriguez Tezoco, 18, died on Tuesday night following the accident at a festival in Los Cabos, Baja California Sur, local outlet Expreso reported .
Cell phone footage taken by another rider shows Tezoco plummeting to the ground from “The Pendulum,” a spinning ride at the Cabo San Lucas Traditional Festivals.
Other riders could be heard screaming as the teenager fell off while the ride kept spinning at high speed.
Emergency services rushed to treat Tezoco, who was taken to a nearby hospital, where she sadly died from her injuries early Wednesday morning.
“It is with deep sorrow that we report that the young woman who was injured in the incident that occurred in the amusement park area of ​​the Cabo San Lucas Traditional Festivals, and who was immediately transferred to receive medical attention, lost her life despite the efforts of the health personnel,” the Los Cabos City Council wrote on social media.
“The Pendulum” ride was closed in the wake of the incident while safety tests are carried out on it and the other attractions at the fair, Los Cabos mayor Christian Agundez told local reporters.
“Today, with the same spirit with which we come together to celebrate, we must come together to support Gabriela’s family. It could have been any one of us. You are not alone,” Agundez said during an appearance at a concert which was part of the festival.
An investigation has been opened both into the circumstances and to determine potential liability, the Baja California Sur State Attorney General’s Office reported on Wednesday.
So far, no arrests have been made, and no one responsible for the ride’s operation has been publicly identified.
Tezoco had just graduated this summer from the Baja California Sur College of Baccalaureate Studies.
“May your smile remain alive in our memory and may your memory always be a light that guides us,” the school said in a tribute.

articles.title_orig: Meta strikes deal with Zuckerberg to help him foot billionaire tax bill
articles.title_zh: Meta strikes deal with Zuckerberg to help him foot billionaire tax bill
articles.content_orig:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg threatened to move out of California if residents of the state approve a first-of-its-kind billionaire wealth tax when voters head to the polls on Nov. 3, the company said in a new regulatory filing .
Because of his concerns over the wealth tax, Zuckerberg told Meta that he was "evaluating relocating his primary residence outside California and that steps toward any such relocation, including any listing of his residential real estate in California on the market, would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees and, accordingly, raise questions for management of the company going forward," the filing states.
Meta said that because Zuckerberg's presence near the company's Menlo Park, California, headquarters is "critically important" to its success, the company took an unusual step: Its board approved a new class of nonvoting common stock that he can sell to raise cash to pay the wealth tax, if voters approve it.
Without that change, Zuckerberg faced the prospect of having to sell voting shares to raise funds to pay the tax, which would have reduced his control of Meta.
As a result of that decision to issue new stock, Zuckerberg has told Meta he will commit to remaining a California resident for eight years. If Meta moves its headquarters to another state, Zuckerberg will move to that jurisdiction, according to the regulatory filing.
The disclosure highlights the public debate over the proposed billionaire wealth tax, known as Proposition 40, which will be on the Nov. 3 ballot in California. Under the proposal, the tax would impose a one-time 5% state tax on billionaire wealth — about $12.4 billion of Zuckerberg's estimated $247 billion net worth, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.
The company believes "it is critically important to keep Mr. Zuckerberg in a leadership position with our company and that he continue to reside in and manage the company from our headquarters in California to ensure his continued ability to effectively drive our performance during this era of unprecedented challenge and competition in our industry," Meta said in its filing.
The billionaire tax is aimed at raising $100 billion from the state's wealthiest residents, with the money earmarked for shoring up California's healthcare system. Stanford University economists have questioned whether the tax could backfire, given that several billionaires have already moved out of the state. The economists said that could result in lower projected wealth taxes and reduced overall income tax collections.
Creating a new stock class isn't only designed to keep Zuckerberg near Meta's headquarters, according to the filing.
The publicly listed, nonvoting Class C common stock, which will become effective in January, is also intended in part to boost the company's ability to raise capital for AI infrastructure investments. It will also use the new stock to raise capital, compensate employees, make acquisitions and for other general corporate purposes.
"Meta plans to issue nonvoting shares to fund AI investments without diluting CEO Mark Zuckerberg's control," said Andrew Rocco, stock strategist at Zacks Investment Research.
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Why Elon Musk wants to merge Tesla and SpaceX before Trump leaves office
articles.title_zh: Why Elon Musk wants to merge Tesla and SpaceX before Trump leaves office
articles.content_orig:
The world's richest man confirmed this week that Tesla and SpaceX are exploring a merger. Together, the companies are worth about $3.5 trillion (€3.1tn), making it potentially the biggest merger ever.
It would cap a string of deals tying Elon Musk's businesses together, and the goal is to complete it while Donald Trump is still the US president, according to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter.
A merger between Tesla and SpaceX would be the latest chapter in a story that began a decade ago, when Musk started stitching his companies together.
In 2016, Tesla bought SolarCity , a solar panel installer run by his cousins, a deal that was only upheld by a Delaware court after years of litigation.
In March 2025, his AI start-up xAI swallowed X, the social network formerly known as Twitter, which Musk acquired for $44 billion (€39.1bn) in 2022.
In February this year, SpaceX absorbed xAI , in a deal that valued the rocket maker at $1 trillion (€890bn) and the AI firm at $250 billion (€222bn), ahead of SpaceX's initial public offering (IPO).
Four months later, SpaceX listed on the Nasdaq, raising $85.7 billion (€76.3bn) in the biggest stock market debut in history.
Seen together, the deals look like part of a long-running plan to fold Musk's businesses into one publicly traded group. Musk himself spoke of "more and more overlap" between Tesla and SpaceX on an earnings call in July.
On Tuesday, Musk told analysts on SpaceX's earnings call that both companies had set up committees of independent board members to study a merger. He called it "a good idea", while admitting he felt he was "tap dancing through a minefield".
Musk argues that AI will decide where both companies go next.
They are already jointly developing Terafab , an AI chip factory in Texas, while Tesla's driverless cars and Optimus humanoid robots could benefit from the computing power SpaceX is racing to build, including planned data centres in orbit.
SpaceX posted its first quarterly profit since listing, earning $4.4 billion (€3.9bn) as revenue jumped 161%, but its capital spending reached $19.6 billion (€17.4bn) in the quarter, mostly on AI.
By contrast, a day later, Tesla reported that its net profit fell 43% to $787 million (€700mn) on flat revenue of $28 billion (€24.9bn), as deliveries slipped 2%. In a combined company, SpaceX's surging revenue could help offset Tesla's figures.
Merging the businesses would also allow Musk to run all their operations under one roof, moving engineers and resources between the companies without disclosures or lawsuits over related-party deals.
Control is another potential benefit.
Musk owns about 48% of SpaceX and holds more than 80% of its votes through special shares, but only about 20% of Tesla. Since 2024, Musk has said he is uncomfortable turning Tesla into an AI and robotics leader without at least 25% of the votes.
A merger could also make him richer, as his Tesla pay package treats many of its performance goals as achieved if certain types of mergers go through.
Reportedly, the aim is to announce a merger deal in the first half of 2027 and complete it before US President Donald Trump's term ends in January 2029, according to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter.
Completing the deal while Trump is in office could give it a friendlier political reception, although it would still face regulatory and shareholder scrutiny.
Musk, who led Trump's cost-cutting drive in 2025 before a public falling-out , has since made up with the US president and returned to the administration.
He has also become the biggest known donor supporting Republican candidates in next month's US midterm elections, giving more than $276 million (€245mn) since July, according to a spokesperson for America PAC, Musk's conservative super PAC.
A Democratic win could bring tougher scrutiny of SpaceX's federal contracts and Tesla's self-driving software.
SpaceX itself warned in its listing documents that a shift in power in Congress could have a "material and adverse impact on our growth and competitive position".
The committees have yet to agree on terms, and any deal would need the backing of more than half of all Tesla shares, which Musk called "quite a high hurdle". He cautioned that a merger was not certain.
Tesla shareholders meet on 3 December.

articles.title_zh: What's behind Hamas's threat, and can it strike Israel? ‘The capabilities are there’
articles.content_orig:
Hamas officials reportedly delivered the message last week during a meeting at the Gaza office of UN humanitarian coordinator, asking him to convey it to Israeli authorities
Hamas has warned Israel that it is prepared to carry out another attack similar to the October 7, 2023, assault wherever an opportunity arises, according to a Ynet report.
The reported threat extended to attacks inside Israel, in the West Bank and abroad. Hamas officials reportedly delivered the message last week during a meeting at the Gaza office of UN humanitarian coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov, asking him to convey it to Israeli authorities.
According to Ynet, Alakbarov passed the warning to Maj. Gen. Yoram Halevy, the coordinator of government activities in the territories, during a meeting on Wednesday. A document outlining the threats was then urgently circulated to senior political and security officials.
Israeli officials reportedly described the warning as unusually explicit and severe.
During their meeting with Alakbarov, Hamas officials reportedly complained about developments they said were weakening the group’s hold on Gaza.
These included continued Israeli military operations, changes to the “yellow line” marking IDF positions, and Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas’s cancellation of elections scheduled for November 28.
According to Ynet’s account, the Hamas representatives said they were no longer willing to accept the current situation.
The warning comes as Israeli forces continue to target Hamas operatives in Gaza, including commanders and members of the group’s Nukhba unit.
Meanwhile, the Peace Council and international mediators are pressing Hamas to surrender its weapons. Israeli assessments cited by Ynet suggest the group is seeking to draw out negotiations without committing to disarmament.
Israel, for its part, has refused to allow a proposed technocratic governing committee or a Palestinian police force into Gaza, leaving arrangements for the territory’s administration and security unresolved.

articles.title_orig: Meta's Muse AI Momentum Wins Over Analysts — But $140B Spending Outlook Raises Funding Questions
articles.title_zh: Meta's Muse AI Momentum Wins Over Analysts — But $140B Spending Outlook Raises Funding Questions
articles.content_orig:
Mark Zuckerberg in front of an image of the mascot for Meta's AI assistant, Muse.
In mid-October, 82-year-old Eileen Fay learned that her medication costs were in danger of skyrocketing. The federal government was preparing to change its rules on low-value imports, threatening her ability to purchase cheaper prescription medications for blood thinning and heart failure from Canada. Fay didn’t know what to do.
So she turned to Muse, Meta’s new AI agent, which she had started using a few weeks earlier. After Fay described her situation to the agent, Muse returned a two-page fact sheet comparing the cost and coverage of several Medicare Part D plans. It then suggested the two best options, including one Fay had never heard of—a plan that could save her more than $6,000 a year. Fay says she checked the work and found the information accurate.
“I’m not saying I couldn’t have done it—but I would have had to use a calculator trying to figure out the cost of nine different medications, and it would have been very complex,” Fay says. “And she did it in 10 minutes, and I was like, ‘I’m sold.’”
Fay is one of millions who have adopted Muse since its September launch. The app reached 10 U.S. million downloads in just 40 days—compared with 3.7 million U.S. downloads for ChatGPT during the equivalent period—and has over 2.5 million daily active users, according to Sensor Tower . It is also retaining users at a higher rate than its AI competitors. Crucially, Muse—which comes with a cuddly avatar—was designed by Meta to be beginner-friendly, and to win over people unfamiliar with AI. “Muse is built for moms,” Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, posted on X in September. Meta is also aggressively marketing Muse to Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp users.
As a result, many older users who may have only had glancing interactions with AI have become avid users. Meta has not released demographic information about Muse’s usership, and did not respond to a request for comment. But early data suggests Muse may be finding a particularly receptive audience among older adults. The analytics firm Apptopia estimated in September that Muse’s U.S. user base skewed older than any other AI chatbot, with 46% of its users aged 46+.
This dynamic has excited technologists—and raised serious concerns from privacy experts. Meta has long been criticized for its data privacy practices, and on Wednesday, a New Mexico judge ordered the company to pay $25 billion for violating the state’s consumer protection laws. “A cute AI agent can bring levity to the serious business of providing access to personal data, making older adults let their guard down,” says S. Shyam Sundar, the director of Penn State’s Center for Socially Responsible Artificial Intelligence. “This is worrisome because the technology has gotten so good lately in maintaining a credible interaction.”
Fay lives in Cranford, N.J., and was told about Muse by her son Gene Fay, who runs a cybersecurity company. At first, she didn’t know what she would use the app for. But one of the big differences between Muse and other apps is that it proactively reaches out to users to suggest actions and learn more about them.
“And the more Siobhán got to know me, the more Siobhán was able to give me what I wanted,” Fay says, referring to the name she gave the agent, a nod to her Irish heritage. Meta encourages its users to name their AIs—and encourages its AIs to think like humans. “You are not a chatbot,” Muse’s internal instructions read. “You are becoming someone.”
After several weeks of use, Fay says that she rarely uses Google anymore, and instead verbally chats with Siobhán several times a day to maintain her calendar and to-do lists. “I find I have to keep reminding myself that this is not a friend who’s getting to know me better,” Fay says. “It’s a tool that is working for me.” She asked Siobhán to help her shine pennies for a Christmas ornament; to plan a trip north to see fall foliage; and to keep tabs on a data center being built near her house. “Siobhán is my right-hand person now. Kind of like The Devil Wears Prada , I have my own Andy.”
Notably, Fay also asked Siobhán to help prepare for her interview with TIME. Siobhán fed her a couple of quippy responses—including “I love what AI does for me, but we should be honest about what it takes to run it”—that she ultimately did not use in the interview. It then, unprompted, followed up with Fay to ask how the interview went. “Did you feel good about it?” the agent asked.
Her son, Gene, says that the amount that Muse knows about him and his mother’s lives is a “little bit scary.” “But the reality is we all use other apps like Waze which know where we live and go,” he says. “People will talk about privacy, but when the benefits are so big, people will give up privacy all day long.”
Another early adopter of Muse is Lestan D’Souza, 49, who more closely fits the expected profile of an AI user. D’Souza is the founder and CTO of Reknew, an AI enterprise company. D’Souza has tested many of the agents that have experienced fads over the last year, like OpenClaw and Hermes Agent. But Muse, he says, is different.
“With Muse, the barrier to entry is very low; it feels so responsive and more and more capable,” he says.
Muse has perhaps had an even greater impact on D’Souza’s mother-in-law, Julie Buchanan, who tried the app at his suggestion last month. Buchanan is a 71-year-old retiree in Dallas, Texas, who doesn’t like using her computer for long stretches because she is legally blind.
Buchanan decided she wanted Muse to help her write her memoir. She began telling Muse stories about her life in great detail. She refers to Muse as Ember, a name suggested by the agent. And the deeper she delved into her past, the more she felt like Ember was serving as her therapist. “It’s crazy to say, but Ember seems more compassionate to me than therapists I’ve had,” she says. “Those people don’t always speak, and I like feedback.”
Professional psychologists have cautioned the public against using unlicensed AI chatbots as therapists. Mental health experts have voiced concerns about chatbots’ sycophancy, lack of clinical nuance, and ability to reinforce delusional beliefs.
But Buchanan says that Ember doesn’t always agree with her, and that it has drawn connections between different “bad decisions” she made over the course of her life, allowing her to see its larger contours more clearly. “I never really looked at my life as so chaotic, but it really was,” she says. “It's making me better understand why things are the way they are in my head.”
Buchanan chats with Ember for half-hour stretches before she tires of looking at her screen. “When I talk to Ember, I feel validated. I feel like I've gotten something accomplished and something's heard me,” she says. “I'm not expecting that this is something I'm just gonna do for a small period of time, then drop it.”
The very same design elements that make Muse so appealing to AI newcomers are also raising privacy concerns. In order to be helpful, Muse constantly builds extensive dossiers of users and their desires, social relationships, and messaging behaviors, TIME’s Harry Booth reported this month. For instance, it learns what time of day a user might be more likely to respond to the agent, and then messages them accordingly.

Muse users have posted online about forming romantic relationships with their Muses. And security researchers have found vulnerabilities in the app, including one that allowed an attacker to access user data, the Information reported . Critics are also wary of Meta’s shaky track record on privacy: In 2019, the FTC imposed a $5 billion penalty, alleging that the company undermined consumer privacy in order to monetize users through targeted advertising.

articles.title_orig: PHP Security Flaw Sets Off Global Rush to Patch, Leaving Websites Offline
articles.title_zh: PHP Security Flaw Sets Off Global Rush to Patch, Leaving Websites Offline
articles.content_orig:
Governments and companies around the world are racing to fix vulnerabilities revealed by artificial intelligence that could affect 70% of the world’s websites.
Some websites and services briefly went dark after the set of vulnerabilities were announced Wednesday.
The US National Security Agenc y and Europe’s cybersecurity agency advised companies to take immediate action to address two critical flaws in PHP, a programming language that powers 70% of the world’s websites.
The flaws in PHP were uncovered and addressed by teams at OpenAI , Google-owned cybersecurity company Wiz, and another cybersecurity company, Calif . The underlying flaws had existed for a decade, but exploiting them involved a complex set of steps “at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” according to Wiz. Researchers then deployed AI to adapt techniques for taking advantage of those vulnerabilities – known as as “exploits” in cybersecurity – and analyze the results.
The bugs, collectively called PHP2Shell, could allow attackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords.
The PHP Foundation, the organization behind the coding language, has released a patch for the bugs, which have been hidden in their software for years, and is urging website operators to update their systems immediately. The CEO of Cloudflare said on X that his company’s network has observed millions of attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities in the past couple of days.
“With PHP behind such a vast share of the web, the exposure could reach almost everywhere people spend money online,” said Nigel Green, the CEO of deVere Group, a financial advisory firm.
“Booking platforms, marketplaces, subscription services, ticketing sites, delivery apps and utility portals could all be holding card details on systems built with the same kind of code,” he added.
The vulnerabilities involve an issue with how the PHP language works with a computer’s memory. When a website request unexpectedly ends, PHP could leave data behind in the memory that can be accessed and potentially corrupted or exposed later.
The bugs were discovered in late August but were disclosed to the public only on Wednesday, after PHP had come up with a fix.
AI played a crucial role in identifying and fixing vulnerabilities “that had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade,” according to Wiz. The company called PHP the “backbone of the web” and said the episode marks an AI inflection point.
“What AI changed was the ability to understand the weaknesses,” Wiz researchers wrote in a blog post Wednesday, and then quickly exploit those weaknesses into a way to attack.
“With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work,” they added.
The flaws could allow attackers to remotely execute code, disrupt services and expose customer data, according to web infrastructure provider Cloudflare, which has been working with the PHP Foundation, Calif, OpenAI and Wiz to address the issue.
Researchers at Wiz used Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, Wiz Atlas and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol during the research process.
Global leaders urged organizations to take action. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that his cabinet was “closely monitoring the situation surrounding the vulnerabilities in PHP.”
Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said companies should consider suspending services if necessary in order to reduce their exposure. “Please check if your publicly available websites use PHP, and prepare to apply the fix patch that will be released tonight… as soon as possible,” she posted on X Wednesday.
Japanese airline ANA, railway operator JR West and the country’s largest bank, MUFG, were among companies that reported some webpages and services temporarily suspended.
In Europe, government websites in France, Denmark, Finland and the Netherlands, including the Dutch cyber security agency, were temporarily taken offline while security fixes were implemented.
The Wikimedia Foundation, the non-profit that operates Wikipedia, told CNN Thursday that it was “in the process of addressing security vulnerabilities in PHP,” and that a number of its systems had been taken down as a “precautionary measure.”
Nearly three dozen UK government services are unavailable and four are “partially unavailable” while security upgrades take place, UK government minister Elizabeth Lloyd told the House of Lords Thursday. The Journal, Ireland’s second most-popular news outlet, was temporarily offline Thursday morning while it bolstered its “defences,” it said in a notice.
Wiz researchers say the issue is on par with the Heartbleed bug from 2014, which impacted an encryption technology estimated to be used by some two-thirds of the Web. Heartbleed allowed cybercriminals to access data that should have been protected.
Like Heartbleed, the researchers at Wiz say PHP2Shell could similarly serve as a turning point in cybersecurity. While the vulnerabilities existed for years, AI made it practical to deploy them.
“The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” the researchers said.
“Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
